paper1_text: Learning how to correctly and effectively use existing APIs is a common task — and a core challenge — in software development. It spans all expertise levels from novices to professional software engineers, and all project types from prototypes to production code. The landscape of publicly available APIs is massive and constantly changing, as new APIs are created in response to shifting programmer needs. Within companies, the same is true, perhaps even more so: joining a company can require learning a whole new set of proprietary APIs before a developer becomes an effective contributor to the company codebase. Developers often are stymied by various learning barriers, including overly specific or overly general explanations of API usage, lack of understanding about the interaction between multiple APIs, lack of alternative uses, and difficulty identifying program statements and structures related to an API [11, 19, 5].
paper2_text: Inexperienced researchers often lack knowledge of the implicit writing conventions and structural expectations of particular communities. While existing writing guides offer general advice, they are often too abstract and high-level, making it challenging for junior researchers to apply this guidance in their own work.
basis: Query paragraph opens paper1's Introduction by motivating the work: learning to use APIs effectively is a common but hard task due to knowledge/learning barriers. Candidate 0 plays the same structural role—opening paper2's Introduction by motivating the work with the problem that novice researchers lack knowledge of implicit writing conventions and existing guides are too abstract. Both paragraphs are the initial 'problem motivation' statement of their respective introductions, framing a learning-barrier problem (API usage vs. writing conventions) that the rest of the paper addresses. No other candidate serves this same opening motivating-problem role.

paper1_text: One study found that the greatest obstacle to learning an API is "insufficient or inadequate examples." [19] Official documentation is typically dominated by textual descriptions and explanations, often lacking concrete code examples that illustrate API usage. Tutorials and blog posts walk developers through simplified code examples but often without demonstrating alternative uses of an API, which programmers frequently desire when learning unfamiliar APIs [5, 19, 4].
paper2_text: Inexperienced researchers often lack knowledge of the implicit writing conventions and structural expectations of particular communities. While existing writing guides offer general advice, they are often too abstract and high-level, making it challenging for junior researchers to apply this guidance in their own work.
basis: The query paragraph motivates the work by citing evidence that lacking good examples is the greatest obstacle to learning an API, paralleling candidate [0]'s motivation that inexperienced researchers lack knowledge of implicit conventions and that existing guides are too abstract to be actionable. Both paragraphs open their respective introductions by identifying a gap between general/textual guidance (writing guides vs. official documentation) and the concrete examples learners actually need. While paper2's paragraph is about writing conventions rather than API examples specifically, it plays the identical structural role as the first motivating problem statement in the introduction, making it the closest match among the candidates. No other candidate paragraph addresses this same 'insufficient examples as the core learning obstacle' framing as directly.

paper1_text: Code-sharing sites like GitHub hold the promise of documenting all the common and uncommon ways of using an API in practice, including many alternative usage scenarios that are not typically shown in curated examples. However, given the large amount of code available online, it is challenging for developers to efficiently browse the enormous volume of search results. It is certainly infeasible for developers to examine more than a few code examples simultaneously. In practice, programmers often investigate a handful of search results and return to their own code due to limited time and attention [3, 23, 5]. Prior work has shown that individual code examples may suffer from API usage violations [29], insecure coding practices [7], unchecked obsolete usage [31], and comprehension difficulties [25]. Therefore, inspecting a few examples may leave out critical safety checks or desirable usage scenarios.
paper2_text: Given that people commonly learn through examples, providing access to relevant examples can help bridge this gap. However, there are obstacles: viewing too few examples may lead to overfitting and unintentional plagiarism, while viewing too many examples—without sufficient cognitive supports within the interface—may overwhelm the writer.
basis: The query paragraph explains the problem of large-scale code repositories being hard to browse, and that viewing too few examples risks missing important patterns/safety issues while too many is infeasible to examine. This mirrors paragraph 1's core tension: 'viewing too few examples may lead to overfitting... while viewing too many examples—without sufficient cognitive supports—may overwhelm the writer.' Both paragraphs establish the same underlying motivation: examples are valuable but there's a fundamental few-vs-many tradeoff that motivates the paper's tool. Paragraph 0 is a related but distinct motivation (abstract writing guides), so paragraph 1 is the closer match for this specific few-vs-many examples argument.

paper1_text: In the software engineering community, there is a growing interest in leveraging a large collection of open source repositories—so-called Big Code—to automatically infer API usage patterns from massive corpora [4, 16, 26, 30]. However, these API usage mining techniques provide limited support to help programmers explore concrete code examples from which API usage patterns are inferred, and understand the commonalities and variances across different uses. To bridge the gap, we aim to visualize hundreds of concrete code examples mined from massive code corpora in a way that reveals their commonalities and variances, and design a navigation model to guide the exploration of these examples. We draw motivation from prior work on visualizing large corpora of related documents, e.g., student coding assignments [8], text [27, 21], and image manipulation tutorials [17], to pose the following research question: How might we extract, align, canonicalize, and display large numbers of usage examples for a given API?
paper2_text: To this end, we implemented CorpusStudio, a writing environment with two novel writing support concepts, one at the document level and one at the sentence level, that help writers learn about the writing styles and expectations of particular audiences. These writing supports are designed to expose writers to as many examples as possible to increase the variety of examples shown to the users—with the cognitive support necessary to help them see the emergent patterns that capture otherwise implicit community-specific writing content and style expectations. Specifically, at the document level, CorpusStudio computes and renders an ordered distribution [15] over section title sequences in prior papers from the community the writer wishes to write for. This gives the writer a sense of common and uncommon section titles and in what relative order they appear in prior papers (Figure 1A). At the sentence level, CorpusStudio retrieves many example sentences from the corpus given the user's draft-in-progress and their current cursor location within it (Figure 1C). Words across these many example sentences are algorithmically highlighted or de-emphasized to help users see any emergent norms and outliers. We also allow authors to capture their thoughts and deductions from viewing these examples with bookmarks and notes.
basis: The query paragraph (paper1, API usage example visualization) motivates the work by identifying a gap—existing tools mine patterns but don't help programmers explore concrete examples—then poses a research question about extracting/aligning/displaying many examples. This is analogous to paper2's paragraph 4, which describes CorpusStudio's approach to surfacing many concrete examples (section titles, sentences) with cognitive support to reveal commonalities/patterns, addressing the gap of too few vs too many examples. However, the closer structural match is actually to paragraph 1/2 which discuss the core problem of examples. Given the query is specifically about the research question and system goal to visualize/extract/align examples, paragraph 4 best corresponds as it describes the system's core mechanism for exposing many examples to reveal emergent patterns, paralleling the query's stated research question of extracting, aligning, canonicalizing, and displaying usage examples.

paper1_text: In this paper, we introduce a novel interactive visualization and navigation technique called EXAMPLORE that (1) gives a bird's-eye view of common and uncommon ways in which a community of developers uses an API and (2) allows developers to quickly filter a corpus for concrete code examples that exhibit these various uses. It operates on hundreds of code examples of a given API method, which can be automatically mined from open-source projects or proprietary codebases. It is designed to supplement existing resources: for example, while Stack Overflow can provide explanations and discussions, EXAMPLORE provides quantitative information about how an API call is used in the wild.
paper2_text: To this end, we implemented CorpusStudio, a writing environment with two novel writing support concepts, one at the document level and one at the sentence level, that help writers learn about the writing styles and expectations of particular audiences. These writing supports are designed to expose writers to as many examples as possible to increase the variety of examples shown to the users—with the cognitive support necessary to help them see the emergent patterns that capture otherwise implicit community-specific writing content and style expectations. We also allow authors to capture their thoughts and deductions from viewing these examples with bookmarks and notes.
basis: Both paragraphs introduce the paper's novel tool and describe its core capabilities. Query introduces EXAMPLORE with its two capabilities (bird's-eye view of common/uncommon API usage, and filtering examples), paralleling paragraph 4's introduction of CorpusStudio with its two novel writing support concepts (document-level distribution view, sentence-level example retrieval). Both frame the tool as operating over large corpora (hundreds of code examples vs. many example sentences/papers) to help users see patterns/norms. This is the closest structural and functional match.

paper1_text: EXAMPLORE instantiates a synthetic code skeleton that captures a variety of API usage features, including initializations, enclosing control structures, guard conditions, and other method calls before and after invoking the given API method, etc. This skeleton is designed to be general: it is grounded in how API design is taught in software engineering curricula and how API mining researchers conceptualize their tasks [11, 19, 5]. EXAMPLORE visualizes the statistical distribution of each API usage feature in the skeleton to provide quantitative evidence of each feature in the corpus. The user can select one or more features in the skeleton and, by dynamically filtering mined code examples from the corpus, drill down to concrete, supporting code examples. Color-coordinated highlighting makes it easier for users to recognize the correspondence between features in the skeleton and code segments within each example.

Candidate 4 plays the same structural role in paper2: it introduces CorpusStudio and describes its two novel writing support concepts (document-level section title distributions and sentence-level example retrieval with highlighting), explaining how the system helps users see emergent patterns and drill into examples—paralleling EXAMPLORE's skeleton-to-example drill-down mechanism. Both paragraphs are the 'here is our system and how it concretely works' paragraph in their respective introductions.

paper1_text: We conducted a within-subjects lab study where we asked sixteen Java programmers of various levels of expertise to answer questions about the usage of particular Java APIs based on either (1) searching online for relevant code examples, blogs, and forum posts or (2) using EXAMPLORE to explore one hundred API usage examples mined from GitHub. On average, participants answered significantly more API usage questions correctly, with more concrete details, using EXAMPLORE. This suggests that EXAMPLORE helps users grasp a more comprehensive view of API usage than online search. In a post survey, the majority of participants (13/16) found EXAMPLORE to be more helpful for answering API usage questions than online search, and when using EXAMPLORE, their median level of confidence in their answers was higher.
paper2_text: We conducted a user study with N=16 participants from the academic community who were actively writing their manuscripts. They used CorpusStudio to draft their paper outline, wrote one to two sections of their manuscript, and answered questionnaires eliciting their overall experience writing within CorpusStudio.
basis: Both paragraphs describe the user study conducted with N=16 participants to evaluate the respective tool (EXAMPLORE vs CorpusStudio) against a baseline (online search vs no tool), including study design and task. Paragraph 5 in paper2 describes the study setup (N=16 participants, using CorpusStudio to draft outlines and write sections), which corresponds to the query's description of the study setup (16 Java programmers, comparing EXAMPLORE vs online search). While the query also reports specific quantitative results (more correct answers, higher confidence) that paper2 candidate 6 partially covers in a different way (previewing key findings), paragraph 5 is the closest structural match as it introduces the study methodology itself, matching the query's core role of describing 'what user study was conducted.'

paper1_text: Our contributions are: • a method for generating an interactive visualization of a distribution of code examples for a given API call • an implementation of this interactive visualization for a set of Java and Android API calls • a within-subjects lab study that shows how this interactive visualization may fill an important role in developers' programming workflows as they use unfamiliar APIs.
paper2_text: In summary, we contribute the following: • We designed two novel writing support concepts that make visible emergent patterns at the document-level and sentence-level of a given paper corpus. • We implemented these writing support concepts within CorpusStudio, an interactive writing environment that helps writers retrieve, inspect, generalize from, and reflect on many examples from their target venue • We found that users' writing goals guided their perception of relevance and how they adapted content from the corpus.
basis: Both paragraphs are the contributions list at the end of the introduction, structured as bullet points summarizing the paper's main contributions (a method/tool implementation plus a user study demonstrating its usefulness). Candidate 7 mirrors this exact rhetorical role for CorpusStudio (design concepts, implementation, study findings), matching the query's contributions list for the API example visualization (method, implementation, lab study).
